areas.name: Big Chiwaukum
areas.blurb: Big Chiwaukum is the highest summit of the Chiwaukum Mountains, the rugged range between Stevens Pass and Leavenworth in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. It sees only a handful of parties each year and is usually climbed as a long day from Whitepine Creek.

areas.name: Stuart Range Traverses
areas.blurb: Multi-peak link-ups across the Stuart Range and the Enchantments. They cross several summits, so they are filed here rather than under any one peak.

areas.name: Glacier Peak Wilderness Traverses
areas.blurb: Multi-peak ridge traverses in the Glacier Peak Wilderness. They cross several summits, so they are filed here rather than under any one peak.

routes.name: Standard Route (Headlee Pass)
routes.rock_grade: Class 2 granite slabs, a few easy hands-on moves
routes.best_season: Late July through September, once the snow has melted out of the Headlee Pass couloir and the upper slabs. Earlier in the season it becomes a snow climb that needs an ice axe and the skill to use it.
routes.overview: The walk-up way to the top of Vesper Peak: a steep trail over Headlee Pass, then a bootpath and open granite slabs to a summit with big views of Big Four, Del Campo and the Monte Cristo peaks. The scrambling is mostly low-angle rock with only light hands-on moves, but it is a long, steep day with real route-finding above treeline.
routes.beta: From the Vesper Creek basin above Headlee Pass, cross Vesper Creek rather than continuing up to Vesper Lake, and pick up the bootpath climbing the far bank through heather, stunted cedars and rock. The path steepens through the last subalpine trees, rocky in places and a slick muddy rut in others. Above treeline the mountain turns to granite: scramble mostly low-angle slabs toward the high point, staying on the subtle central rib. Gullies lie to the left and steep, exposed terrain drops away to the right, so if the ground suddenly gets harder you have drifted off the rib. A steep snowfield can linger near the summit into summer; it can be bypassed on the left.
routes.approach: From the Sunrise Mine trailhead, Trail 707 crosses several streams in the first mile, including the main South Fork Stillaguamish, which has no bridge and can be a serious obstacle when runoff is high. The trail then climbs through forest and an open talus basin before tightening into steep, narrow switchbacks up the couloir to Headlee Pass, about 2.7 miles from the trailhead. From the pass, the trail traverses the south flank of Sperry Peak into the upper Vesper Creek basin, where the route leaves the lake trail at the creek crossing.
routes.descent_text: Descend the same way. Take care to find the central rib again on the slabs, since the gullies to the descender's right lead into steeper ground, and go slowly down the loose Headlee Pass couloir.
routes.turnaround: Turn around if the upper slabs are wet, icy or in cloud and you cannot see the rib, or if the lingering summit snowfield is hard and you have no axe. Leave enough daylight to get back down the Headlee Pass couloir and across the river before dark.
routes.bail: Retreat is simply reversing the route; there is no other way off. Vesper Lake and the basin below the pass make a sheltered fallback if the summit is out.
gear: Helmet for the Headlee Pass couloir
what_to_bring: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful Pass
Map and navigation for above treeline
Plenty of water or a filter
hazards: The South Fork Stillaguamish crossing has no bridge and can be dangerous in high runoff.
Rockfall in the narrow Headlee Pass couloir, often knocked down by other parties above.
Falls of 10-20 feet are possible on the upper slabs.
Steep, exposed terrain on the east side of the summit block.
A steep snowfield can linger near the summit into summer.
routes.watch_out:
Do not follow the trail on to Vesper Lake; the summit route leaves it at the Vesper Creek crossing.
Staying on the central rib keeps the scrambling easy; drifting right puts you on exposed ground.
Granite slabs become very slick when wet.
Keep spacing in the Headlee Pass couloir so nobody is directly below you.
pro_tips: Start early on summer weekends; the trailhead lot fills and the couloir is safer with fewer people above you.
Note where you came up onto the slabs so you can find the bootpath again on the way down.
Check the river level before committing; it is usually lower in the morning.

road.name: Mountain Loop Highway to Sunrise Mine Road (FR 4065)
road.driveNote: From Granite Falls, drive the Mountain Loop Highway east about 28 miles, then turn right onto Sunrise Mine Road (FR 4065) and follow it about 2.3-2.5 miles to its end at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful Pass is required to park.

access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful Pass

routes.name: West Ridge via Wildhorse Creek
routes.rock_grade: Class 2-3 blocky ledges, exposed near the top
routes.best_season: Mid-July through September, once the snow has melted off the upper west slopes. July brings wildflowers to the Wildhorse meadows; September brings fall color, but the streams higher up may be dry.
routes.overview: A long, quiet day to the highest point of the Chiwaukum Mountains. Good trail climbs Whitepine and Wildhorse Creeks, then open meadows and rock bands lead to the west ridge and a short, exposed scramble up blocky ledges to the summit pinnacle.
routes.beta: Leave the Wildhorse Creek Trail at about 5,400 ft, directly west of the summit. Climb east through meadows, going around the rock bands rather than through them, to gain the west ridge. Follow the ridge east toward the main summit ridge. Short of the summit headwall, turn north and traverse below it, then scramble up blocky Class 2-3 ledges to the summit pinnacle. The last moves are exposed; pick the easiest line and test holds, as the rock is broken and loose in places.
routes.approach: From the Whitepine Creek Trailhead (about 2,800 ft), follow Whitepine Creek Trail #1582 up the valley for about 2.5 miles to the junction with Wildhorse Creek Trail #1592. Bear left onto the Wildhorse Creek Trail and climb through forest into the Wildhorse basin to about 5,400 ft, where the trail passes directly west of the summit. Leave the trail here.
routes.descent_text: Reverse the route: down the summit ledges to below the headwall, back west along the west ridge, then down through the meadows to rejoin the Wildhorse Creek Trail, and out the Whitepine Creek Trail to the car.
routes.turnaround: Aim to be on the summit by early afternoon. The descent to the trail and the long walk out take most of the rest of the day, and the ledges are no place to be route-finding in the dark.
routes.bail: You can leave the west ridge at almost any point by descending back west through the meadows to the Wildhorse Creek Trail. If the summit ledges are wet, icy or snow-covered, stop below the headwall.
gear: Ice axe early in the season
what_to_bring: Plenty of water or a filter (streams up high dry up by late summer)
Map and compass or GPS for the off-trail section
Free Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, filled out at the trailhead
hazards: The final ledges to the summit are exposed.
Loose rock and scree on the upper mountain.
Snow lingers on the upper west slopes into July.
A very long day with little water high up late in the season.
routes.watch_out:
Do not try to climb straight up through the rock bands on the west slope; go around them.
Stay below the summit headwall on the traverse north rather than climbing into it.
Parties above you on the ledges can knock rock down.
pro_tips: Start at first light; most parties take 11-13 hours car to car.
Note where you left the trail so you can find it again on the way down.
Fill up on water in the Wildhorse basin before heading off-trail.

road.name: White Pine Road (FR 6950)
road.driveNote: From US-2 about 21.5 miles west of Leavenworth (roughly 13 miles east of Stevens Pass), turn onto White Pine Road (FR 6950) and follow about 4 miles of unpaved road to the trailhead at its end. There are no restrooms or water at the trailhead. Check the trailhead signboard for current parking pass requirements.

access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Wenatchee River Ranger District (Alpine Lakes Wilderness)
access.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, filled out at the trailhead

routes.name: Inspiration Traverse
routes.rock_grade: Mostly 3rd-4th class with low-5th summit blocks; one short, hard boulder-style move (5.7-5.9) on Dorado Needle
routes.best_season: July to early August, while snow bridges over crevasses and moats are still solid
routes.overview: A glaciated high traverse through the heart of the North Cascades that links five of the range's big summits: Eldorado Peak, Dorado Needle, Klawatti Peak, Austera Peak and Primus Peak. This version starts and ends at the Eldorado Creek trailhead on the Cascade River Road, crossing the Eldorado, Inspiration, McAllister and Klawatti glaciers out to Primus and back. It is serious, committing terrain: crevassed ice, steep snow, moats and short, exposed rock summit blocks, far from any easy exit.
routes.beta: From high camp on the edge of the Inspiration Glacier, the peaks can be taken in any order, but a common plan is Eldorado first (a short climb up the snow of its East Ridge to an exposed, knife-edge snow crest at the summit), then east across the Inspiration Glacier to camp at the rock col on the south side of Klawatti. From there, continue over the Klawatti Glacier and the North Klawatti Glacier to Primus, whose south side is easy snow, slabs and mostly stable talus, reaching the south ridge a short way below the top. Austera, reached from the Klawatti/Austera glacier side, has a snowy ridge between its false and true summits and then a short chimney with 4th-class to low-5th mantle moves; most parties belay it and rappel once. Klawatti is climbed from the col on its south side: cross the moat, climb a steep gully with several 4th-class moves (or two or three short low-5th pitches on the southwest buttress), then scramble loose rock and an easy ridge to the long summit; descend with a rappel back over the moat. Dorado Needle is reached from the McAllister Glacier side: gain the ridge north of the peak, then follow an exposed knife-edge ridge that is crossed au cheval to a tiny summit, where the final move is a short, awkward boulder problem up an angled crack in a steep step (about 5.7-5.9). Descend by rappel rather than re-crossing the knife edge, then return over the Inspiration and Eldorado glaciers to the car.
routes.approach: From the Eldorado Creek trailhead on the Cascade River Road, walk a short way down the road and cross the Cascade River on a log. A steep climbers' trail then gains roughly 1,800 ft through forest to a large boulder field around 4,000 ft. Cross the boulder field and Eldorado Creek into the open Eldorado Creek basin, climb to a notch on the ridge above, and drop into the Roush Creek basin at the foot of the Eldorado Glacier. Rope up and climb the Eldorado Glacier north to the broad, flat Inspiration Glacier, where the usual high camp sits on rock at the glacier's edge below Eldorado's East Ridge.
routes.descent_text: Reverse the approach: from the Klawatti col camp or the Inspiration Glacier high camp, cross back over the Inspiration Glacier, descend the Eldorado Glacier to the Roush Creek basin, climb back over the notch into the Eldorado Creek basin, then descend the boulder field and the steep forest trail to the Cascade River log crossing and the car. The boulder field and the steep, rooty trail below it are slow and hard on tired legs.
routes.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround for each summit block so the whole party is back on the glacier before the afternoon snow turns soft over crevasses and moats; if the glaciers are already soft or bridges look thin, drop the remaining peaks rather than pushing on.
routes.bail: The quickest retreat from anywhere on the traverse is back west across the Inspiration Glacier to the Eldorado Glacier and out the approach trail. Each outlying peak (Primus, Austera, Klawatti, Dorado Needle) is a side trip from the glacier and can be skipped. The alternative exit east down to Thunder Creek and the North Cascades Highway ends at a different road and involves a long, rough descent and a big log crossing, so it is not a practical bail for a car parked on the Cascade River Road.
routes.itinerary: Day 1: Hike and scramble from the Eldorado Creek trailhead up the boulder field and basins, climb the Eldorado Glacier and camp on rock at the edge of the Inspiration Glacier; climb Eldorado in the evening if time and conditions allow. Day 2: Cross the Inspiration Glacier east, climb Austera and Primus via the Klawatti and North Klawatti glaciers, and climb Klawatti from the col camp on its south side. Day 3: Climb Dorado Needle from the McAllister Glacier side, then return over the Inspiration and Eldorado glaciers and descend to the car. Many parties add a fourth day, or split the peaks differently, especially when snow is soft or the moats are open.

pitch_detail.notes: Log crossing of the Cascade River, steep forest trail to a large boulder field, then the Eldorado Creek basin and a notch into the Roush Creek basin.
Rope up for the crevassed Eldorado Glacier and continue to the flat Inspiration Glacier; camp on rock at the glacier's edge.
Snow up the East Ridge to an exposed, knife-edge snow crest at the summit. Crampons useful for the descent when firm.
Traverse east across the Inspiration Glacier to the rock col on the south side of Klawatti, a good camp with running water.
Snowy ridge between the false and true summits, then a short chimney with mantle moves and an exposed scramble. Usually belayed; one rappel on the way down.

pitch_detail.pitch: Klawatti and North Klawatti glaciers to Primus
pitch_detail.notes: Cross the Klawatti and North Klawatti glaciers, passing near icefalls.
Snow, slabs and mostly stable talus up the south side to the south ridge just below the summit. Some loose rock on the approach.

From the south-side col, cross the moat and climb a steep gully (several 4th-class moves) or two to three short low-5th pitches, then scramble loose rock to the long summit. Rappel back over the moat.
Cross toward the McAllister Glacier and gain the ridge north of Dorado Needle; crevasses are often the worst of the trip here.
Exposed knife-edge ridge crossed au cheval to a tiny summit; the last move is a short, awkward boulder problem up an angled crack (about 5.7-5.9). Descend by rappel rather than re-crossing the ridge.
Back over the Inspiration and Eldorado glaciers, the notch, the boulder field and the steep forest trail to the car.

gear: Slings and cord for rappel anchors
what_to_bring: Tent that can be pitched on rock or snow
Stove and fuel for melting snow
Navigation for whiteout on the glaciers
hazards: Crevasses
Moats and bergschrunds at the base of summit blocks
Steep snow
Exposed knife-edge ridges
Loose rock
Whiteout on large, featureless glaciers
obj_haz: Crevasses on the Eldorado, Inspiration, McAllister and Klawatti glaciers
Open moats below Klawatti and Austera late in the season
Rockfall and loose rock on Klawatti and the Primus approach
Rime or verglas on summit rock after a storm
routes.watch_out:
Snow bridges and moats deteriorate quickly from mid-July; be on the glaciers early
The Dorado Needle summit move is harder than the rest of the rock; be ready to belay it
Fog can close in over the flat Inspiration Glacier with little warning
The boulder field and forest trail are slow and tiring on the way out
pro_tips: Camp at the rock col on the south side of Klawatti to shorten the days to Austera, Primus and Klawatti
Descend Dorado Needle by rappel instead of re-crossing the knife-edge ridge
Bring extra webbing and a rap ring or two to back up existing rappel anchors
Get on the snow early so crevasse bridges and moat crossings are still firm

road.name: Cascade River Road
road.driveNote: Drive the Cascade River Road east from Marblemount to the Eldorado Creek trailhead pullout at about milepost 20. The trail starts by crossing the Cascade River on a log a short way downstream of the parking.

timing.recommendedStart: Early morning on each glacier day, to cross snow bridges and moats while the snow is still firm

bivy.name: Eldorado Creek basin
bivy.notes: Open basin above the boulder field; a lower camp for parties splitting the approach.

bivy.name: Inspiration Glacier high camp
bivy.notes: Rock outcrops at the edge of the Inspiration Glacier below Eldorado's East Ridge. The standard base for Eldorado and the start of the traverse.

bivy.name: Klawatti col
bivy.notes: Rock tent sites on the col below the south side of Klawatti Peak with running water and big views; well placed for Klawatti, Austera and Primus.

routes.rope_note: One glacier rope for the team, also used to belay and rappel the short summit blocks. A 60 m rope covers the single rappels on Austera and Klawatti; a longer rope gives more margin for rappelling Dorado Needle.
rack: A few small to medium cams
Cord or webbing to back up rappel anchors
Pickets for steep snow and crevasse rescue
An ice screw or two for crevasse rescue
routes.pro_needs: A light rack is enough for belaying the short 4th and low-5th summit blocks and the Dorado Needle boulder move. Carry spare webbing to back up fixed rappel anchors.

access.permit: Overnight backcountry permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, picked up in person in Marblemount
access.fees: $10 per person plus a $6 fee in the summer season (mid-May to early October); youth 15 and under free

routes.name: Enchantment Enchainment
routes.rock_grade: Several pitches of 5.3-5.6 rock; much loose 3rd and 4th class
routes.season: Late June to early October, once Eightmile Road is open and the high snow has consolidated or melted
routes.best_season: July to September. Early season brings steep, hard snow on the gullies and notches (axe and crampons needed); late summer is mostly dry rock and talus.
routes.overview: A car-to-car loop from the Stuart Lake trailhead that links the nine tallest summits of the Enchantments area: Mount Stuart, Sherpa, Argonaut, Colchuck, Dragontail, Little Annapurna, McClellan, Enchantment Peak and Cannon Mountain. It is about 27 miles and roughly 18,000 ft of gain over steep snow, several pitches of low-fifth-class rock and a very large amount of loose 3rd and 4th class scrambling. It is an enchainment rather than a true ridge traverse: the line leaves the crest wherever easier ground links one summit to the next.
routes.beta: Peak order and exact lines are up to the party; the loop below runs west to east. STUART: from the Stuart Lake valley climb slopes toward Long Pass, then steep snow to a notch at about 7,950 ft on the northwest face; drop slightly, traverse snow to a gully that shortcuts onto the upper West Ridge (continuous snow early season, with 3rd class rock beside it), then follow the West Ridge to the summit. The West Ridge is a notorious route-finding trap that benights parties climbing it for the first time, so know the line before you go. SHERPA: descend the upper Cascadian Couloir and cut east to the Stuart-Sherpa col (a short 4th class downclimb on the way), then climb Sherpa's West Ridge, keeping left of the steeper cracks on easier ground. Leave Sherpa by the north side: a short 4th/5th class downclimb, then trend skier's left through a scrambly gully to a large vegetated ledge near 8,100 ft, and on down a broader gully to about 7,200 ft. SHERPA TO ARGONAUT: a long, time-consuming traverse across high granite slabs and goat paths to Argonaut's south-side gullies; the alternative is to drop to the valley trail and climb back up. ARGONAUT: ascend the southern gullies on easy ground to just below the east ridge, with a short easy-fifth-class step to the summit; descend by rappel down the east face. COLCHUCK AND DRAGONTAIL: gain the Colchuck-Dragontail col and tag each summit by its scramble from the col, then descend to Aasgard Pass. THE CORE: from Aasgard Pass continue into the upper Enchantment basin for Little Annapurna (a walk-up from the basin), McClellan Peak (loose scrambling), then Enchantment Peak via Prusik Pass (talus, with a 4th class summit pillar; it has two summits of similar height, so tag both if in doubt) and finally Cannon Mountain from the Enchantment side.
routes.approach: From the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road, follow the Stuart Lake trail up Mountaineer Creek through old burn toward Stuart Lake. Beyond the lake leave the trail and climb the slopes toward Long Pass, then steep snow to the notch on Stuart's northwest face that gives the shortcut onto the upper West Ridge. The West Ridge is normally approached from the south, so this north-side access sees little traffic; expect snow in the notch and gully well into summer.
routes.descent_text: Two ways out from Cannon. The direct line drops north off Cannon straight toward the Stuart Lake trail and the trailhead: roughly 5,000 vertical ft of loose dirt, talus and cliff bands in the upper half, then steep brush and unmapped cliff bands in the lower 2,000 ft, which is slow and miserable, especially in the dark. The longer but known alternative is to return across the Core to Aasgard Pass and descend to Colchuck Lake and the trail back to the trailhead.
routes.turnaround: Set a firm time on Stuart's summit: if the West Ridge has taken much longer than planned, there are still eight summits and the whole Sherpa-Argonaut traverse ahead. A second decision point is Argonaut; past it the terrain is far better travelled.
routes.bail: From Stuart, descend the Cascadian Couloir to Ingalls Creek (south side, away from the car) or retreat the way you came. Between Sherpa and Argonaut, drop north to the valley and the Stuart Lake trail. From Colchuck or Dragontail, descend to Colchuck Lake and the trail out. From anywhere in the Core, Aasgard Pass leads back down to Colchuck Lake and the trailhead.
routes.itinerary: Most parties take two or three days, and the Enchantment overnight permit decides how. Without a lottery permit nobody may camp inside the permit zone (Stuart Lake, Colchuck Lake, the Core and the rest of the zone), so an unpermitted party must either do the whole loop in a single push or split it into separate day trips from the Stuart Lake trailhead, for example Stuart, Sherpa and Argonaut on one day, then Colchuck, Dragontail, Little Annapurna, McClellan, Enchantment Peak and Cannon on another. With an overnight permit, a common split is Stuart, Sherpa and Argonaut on day one with a camp in the permitted zone (Colchuck Lake or the Core), then the Colchuck-Dragontail col and the Core summits over the next one or two days before exiting.

pitch_detail.notes: Stuart Lake trail from the trailhead, then off-trail toward Long Pass and steep snow to the 7,950 ft notch on Stuart's northwest face.
Short drop and snow traverse from the notch to a gully that reaches the upper West Ridge; scramble the rock beside it if the snow is hard.
Upper West Ridge to the true summit. Complex route-finding; many first-time parties lose hours here.
Down the top of the Cascadian Couloir, then east to the col, with a short 4th class downclimb.
Stay on the easier ground left of the steeper cracks.
Short downclimb off the north side, skier's left through a gully to a big vegetated ledge near 8,100 ft, then a broader gully to about 7,200 ft.
Long, time-consuming traverse across high granite slabs and goat paths to Argonaut's south gullies.
Easy south gullies to below the east ridge, then a short easy-fifth step to the summit.
Rappel route down the east face, with a tricky section near the base.
Gain the Colchuck-Dragontail col and scramble to the summit.
From the col to the summit, then down to Aasgard Pass.
Walk-up from the upper Enchantment basin.
Loose scrambling from the Core.
Via Prusik Pass; talus and snow to a short 4th class summit pillar. Two summits of similar height.
From the Enchantment side.
Either straight north off Cannon toward the Stuart Lake trail (about 5,000 ft of loose ground, cliff bands and brush), or back across the Core to Aasgard Pass, Colchuck Lake and the trail.

gear: Light rope for rappels and the fifth-class steps
what_to_bring: Enough food for a very long day
hazards: Steep, hard snow early in the season
Loose 3rd and 4th class terrain nearly the whole way
Route-finding on Stuart's West Ridge
Rockfall in gullies
Thunderstorms on exposed summits
Unmapped cliff bands and brush on the direct descent off Cannon
routes.watch_out:
Stuart's West Ridge benights parties who have not studied it
The Sherpa-to-Argonaut traverse is slow going
The direct descent off Cannon crosses cliff bands a topo map does not show
Camping inside the Enchantment permit zone without a lottery permit is not allowed
pro_tips: Start well before dawn so the steep snow on Stuart is climbed in daylight
Rehearse the fifth-class sections, above all the Stuart West Ridge, before trying the full loop
Everything after Argonaut is on well-travelled ground, so the hard route-finding is front-loaded
Tread lightly on the alpine plants in the Core; stay on rock and snow

road.name: Icicle Creek Road / Eightmile Road (FR 7601)
road.driveNote: From US 2 at the west end of Leavenworth, take Icicle Creek Road 8.4 miles and turn left on Eightmile Road (FR 7601), a rough, potholed dirt road, for about 3.7 miles to the Stuart Lake trailhead at its end. The road is normally closed by snow from November to May. Parking between the Eightmile Lake and Stuart Lake trailheads is on the right side of the road only.

timing.recommendedStart: Pre-dawn, early enough to reach the steep snow on Stuart's northwest side with first light

routes.rope_note: Some parties solo it, but the Argonaut descent is a rappel route and Stuart's West Ridge and Sherpa both have fifth-class steps, so most parties carry a light rope.
rack: A few small to medium cams
Cord for backing up rappel anchors
routes.pro_needs: Light: a handful of pieces for short fifth-class steps and to back up rappel anchors.

access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Alpine Lakes Wilderness
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency (America the Beautiful) pass
access.permit: Enchantment Permit Area. DAY USE: free, self-issued wilderness permit filled out at the trailhead. OVERNIGHT (May 15 to October 31): an Enchantment overnight permit for one zone (Core Enchantment, Colchuck Lake, Stuart Lake, Snow Lake or Eightmile/Caroline), allocated by an advance lottery with leftover dates released later; camping in the permit area without one is prohibited.
access.fees: Day use free. Overnight: $6 non-refundable lottery application fee plus $5 per person per day.

routes.name: Painted Traverse
routes.rock_grade: Mostly class 2-3 ridge with class 4 on Black Mountain; loose gullies
routes.best_season: Late July to early September, once the ridge is mostly snow-free
routes.overview: A long, colorful ridge traverse in the Glacier Peak Wilderness linking Painted Mountain, Magenta Peak, Black Mountain, Skullcap Peak, Portal Peak and White Mountain above the North Fork Sauk valley. Most of the line is heather, meadow and broken ridge, but gendarmes between Magenta and Black force committing route-finding and class 3-4 scrambling on loose rock. It is done as a loop from the North Fork Sauk trailhead, climbing steeply to Painted Mountain and returning from White Pass on the North Fork Sauk Trail.
routes.beta: From the summit of Painted Mountain, follow the crest east over broken ridge and snowfields to Magenta Peak. The section from Magenta to Black Mountain is the crux: the ridge is cut by numerous gendarmes that push you off the crest to find bypasses, with at least one awkward mossy downclimb. Black Mountain, the high point of the route, is climbed through loose scree gullies on its southeast side, and the summit block involves class 4 moves on sometimes slabby rock. Descend Black to the north over lingering snow (typically under about 30 degrees late season) into the basin toward Brown Peak, whose summit can be skipped by crossing its shoulder. Continue south to the base of Skullcap Peak and tag it, then follow easier ridge with decent use paths over the Purple Peak area to Portal Peak. Drop to Red Pass on the Pacific Crest Trail and follow the crest to White Mountain, whose south ridge has a climber's path. Descend to White Pass.
routes.approach: From the North Fork Sauk trailhead, the Red Mountain (Painted Mountain Lookout) Trail branches left about 100 yards in and climbs about a mile to the old lookout site near 3,100 ft. Beyond it an unmaintained climber's path goes straight up the slope with almost no switchbacks, including a short cliff band that needs class 3 scrambling, and continues steeply to the summit of Painted Mountain. Expect close to 5,000 ft of gain in under three miles.
routes.descent_text: From White Mountain descend its south ridge to White Pass on the Pacific Crest Trail, then follow the North Fork Sauk Trail down switchbacks and through old-growth forest back to the trailhead. Parties that stop at Portal Peak can instead drop to Red Pass and take the same trail down.
routes.turnaround: If you have not reached Black Mountain by early afternoon, the remaining ridge is too long to finish in daylight; plan to camp near Black or bail.
routes.bail: Escape options are limited on the western half. From Portal Peak onward, Red Pass and White Pass give easy access to the Pacific Crest Trail and the North Fork Sauk Trail. Reversing to Painted Mountain and down the climber's path is the only straightforward retreat before Black Mountain.
routes.itinerary: Very fit, fast parties do it in a single long day starting before dawn; most parties take two to three days, camping near Black Mountain where water is most reliable.

pitch_detail.notes: Maintained trail to the old lookout site, then a very steep unmaintained path with a short class 3 cliff band to the summit.
Broken ridge, heather and snowfields.
Crux. Numerous gendarmes force off-ridge bypasses, a mossy downclimb, and loose scree gullies on Black's southeast side; class 4 summit block.
Snow descent on the north side of Black, then the basin toward Brown Peak's shoulder and south to Skullcap.
Simpler ridge travel with use paths; short class 3 if Purple Peak is tagged.
Down to Red Pass and along the Pacific Crest Trail, then the climber's path up White Mountain's south ridge.
North Fork Sauk Trail down switchbacks and through forest.

gear: Ice axe and microspikes or crampons before mid-summer or when steep snow remains
what_to_bring: Enough water capacity for long dry stretches
Overnight gear if not doing it in a day
hazards: Loose rock and scree gullies on Black Mountain
Class 4 scrambling on Black Mountain's summit block

Lingering steep snow early in the season, including near Red Pass
Wet heather side-hilling after rain
obj_haz: Exposure to weather on a long ridge with little shelter
routes.watch_out:
Water is scarce late in the season; the only dependable sources are around Black Mountain
Bypasses around gendarmes can lead onto cliffy, loose terrain
Limited bail options before Portal Peak
pro_tips: Going from Painted toward White means climbing, not descending, the loose gullies on Black and the steep climber's path on Painted
Wait for the ridge to be mostly snow-free and dry
Tagging Brown Peak is optional; crossing its shoulder saves time
Load a track before you go; route-finding, not difficulty, is what slows most parties

road.name: Mountain Loop Highway to Sloan Creek Road (FR 49)
road.status: Open seasonally; check Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie road alerts
road.driveNote: From Darrington, drive about 16 miles southeast on the Mountain Loop Highway (mostly gravel on this stretch), turn onto Sloan Creek Road (FR 49) and follow it 6.6 miles to the North Fork Sauk trailhead. The road is potholed and slow.

timing.recommendedStart: Before 4 AM for a single-day push

access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Glacier Peak Wilderness)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass for parking; Glacier Peak Wilderness regulations apply
access.fees: $5 per day or $30 annual Northwest Forest Pass
